title: Design and fabrication of vibration based energy harvester using microelectromechanical system piezoelectric cantilever for low power applications.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The rapidly decreasing cost, size, and power consumption of electronic devices has opened up avenues of research in the developing field of energy harvesting. Energy harvesting from the environment has been actively explored using solar power, wind force, thermal gradients, and vibration energy.1–4 Vibration energy has been examined by many research groups, and the technique of vibration energy harvesting could be applied to ubiquitous/wireless sensor network (USN/WSN), remote systems, and embedded systems for power sources. Piezoelectric materials have been widely used for vibration energy-harvesting devices with microelectromechanical system (MEMS)-scale cantilever beams because they can efficiently convert mechanical strain energy into electrical energy without additional power sources of low power applications.5 Although there have been many successful demonstrations of bulk-scale piezoelectric energy-harvesting prototypes,2 there are relatively few reports on micromachined piezoelectric cantilevers that possess a resonant frequency range between $6 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ .5- 6

The resonant frequency is one of the most important parameters in an energy-harvesting device because the maximum output power density is extracted at the resonant frequency of the piezoelectric resonator. Another important issue in an energy-harvesting device is the maximum output power density. The mechanical strain of the cantilever beam has been said to be the most sensitive factor affecting energy harvesting,7 and the strain distribution can be affected by varying the cantilever beam.8 Therefore, in order to improve the power density and decrease the resonant frequency, we report our investigations of a dual-beam-type cantilever.

Based on power and strain simulation results, we designed and fabricated $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { Z r } , \mathrm { T i } ) { \ r O } _ { 3 }$ (PZT) unimorph cantilevers that possess a large area Si proof mass. The design stage of the cantilever production was aided by the use of a commercial finite element method (FEM) at the MEMS scale, while the fabricated devices can be used in lowfrequency energy-harvesting applications. We also show that there is good agreement between experimentally measured and simulated results.

sections.heading: 2.1. Fabrication Process
sections.text:
A MEMS fabrication process mainly consists of thin film deposition and pattern etching. An inductively-coupled plasma reactive ion etching (ICP RIE) system and a deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) system were used to etch out several layers and release the cantilever beam with the Si proof mass. A $\mathrm { X e F } _ { 2 }$ etching system was used to release the cantilever beam and proof mass.9 $\mathrm { X e F } _ { 2 }$ vapor etching shows high selectivity between the Si and other layers. A silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer was used, and the buried $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer was applied as an etching stop layer.

We used a $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { m m } \ S \mathrm { O I }$ wafer as a substrate. The thicknesses of the first silicon layer, the thermal silicon dioxide layer, and the second silicon layer were $1 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ , and $5 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. $\mathrm { A }$ $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$ d by Publishing Techfilm was grown, to a thickness of about $5 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ , on both sides of each SOI wafer. The $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ on the front surface was used to balance the inertial stress of the PZT film, and the dioxide on the backside surface was used to mask the areas of the surface to prevent damage during the etching of the backside. The interlayer Ti $( 1 0 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ and bottom electrode Pt $\mathrm { 1 0 0 ~ n m } )$ were deposited sequentially by magnetron sputtering without breaking the vacuum. Ti was used for better adhesion between the oxide substrate and the bottom $\mathrm { P t }$ electrode. The PZT was coated using the sol–gel method until it reached a thickness of $1 . 2 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The top electrode was deposited by magnetron sputtering. Finally, $\mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { P Z T } / \mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { T i } / \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ multilayered films were deposited on the SOI substrate. The cantilever with an integrated silicon proof mass was released after the backside $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ and Si films. The structure of the device is shown in Figure 1. To fabricate the device, several plasma etch processes were used. Pt and PZT etch processes were carried out using an inductively-coupled plasma etcher.10- 11 The backside proof mass was patterned using a backside mask of photoresist (PR; AZ-9260). The Si and $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ etch processes were carried out using a DRIE system. It is well known that the DRIE process can cause thermal damage during processing. Therefore, to minimize such damage, the $\mathrm { X e F } _ { 2 }$ etching process was also applied. This fabrication process proved difficult; however, we successfully fabricated the clear shapes of cantilever devices using the above mentioned MEMS process. Subsequently, we were able to corroborate the findings of previously reported experimental work.12

sections.heading: 2.3. Measurements
sections.text:
The dimensions and morphology of the cantilever devices were measured using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, TESCAN). The resonant frequency and output displacement of the fabricated device were measured using a dynamic signal analyzer (DSA) (35670A, Agilent) and a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV; OFV-501, Polytec). A diagram illustrating the measurement equipment is provided elsewhere.12 The cantilever device was mounted on a vibrator. A sine-wave signal was generated from the DSA and used as the vibration source. The DSA and an amplifier controlled the vibration frequency and acceleration, respectively. The acceleration amplitude was monitored by an accelerometer that was mounted on the vibrator. To determine the resonant frequency, the LDV was used to measure the displacement of the cantilever. The DSA recorded the voltages of the measured displacements with acceleration amplitude. These recorded values were displayed on the Bode plot form of the DSA, and the resonant frequency was confirmed from the resulting plot. To measure the output voltage, a resistive load was connected to the device, and the DSA recorded the voltage measured across the resistive Copyright: Americaload. Each output voltage from the device was then systematically measured for different vibration accelerations, vibration frequencies, and resistive loads.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Beam length has a large effect on the resonant frequency. Using the FEM, we simulated the resonant frequency and mechanical strain of a cantilever consisting of Si and PZT films with a Si proof mass. Modal analysis was applied to find the resonant frequency, and harmonic analysis methods were used to estimate the average power.7- 8 The simulation results of voltage and average power are shown in Figure 2. According to simulation, the resonant frequency, voltage, and average power of the dual-beam cantilever were $6 9 . 1 \mathrm { H z }$ , $1 1 3 . 9 \mathrm { m V } ,$ and $0 . 3 0 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ , respectively, at an optimal resistance and at $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { g }$ (gravitational acceleration, $9 . 8 \mathrm { \ m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Therefore, the differences between the simulated and measured values are approximately $12 \%$ . This discrepancy is mainly attributed to model simplification (i.e., ignoring several thin layers). Thus, the simulation results are considered to be in good agreement with the measured values. The simulated resonant frequencies, at a fixed volume, for various beam lengths, are shown in Table I. The data show that as the dual-beam cantilever lengths increase from $4 . 5 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ to $6 . 0 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , and the resonant frequency decreases from $1 0 9 . 1 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $6 3 . 7 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ (keeping the width fixed). The increase in the beam length of the cantilever reduced the effective spring constant,13- 14 where this variable has a close association with the bending modulus per unit width.13 As a result, an increase in beam length leads to a decrease in resonant frequency. This indicates that an increase in beam length is useful for lowering the resonant frequency of a cantilever. Based on our simulations, we selected a beam length of about $5 4 0 0 + 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ in order to decrease the resonant frequency to below $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . This is because the natural frequency extracted from the surroundings should be below $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } . ^ 5 , ( $ We know that to achieve a lower resonant frequency, the cantilever should be lengthened. sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
We designed a PZT cantilever for a realatively high energy density and low resonant frequency on the MEMS scale, with an integrated Si proof mass. The low resonant frequency of the multilayer composite cantilevers were simulated using FEM, and a parametric analysis was carried out in the design process. According to the simulation results, the resonant frequency, voltage, and average power of the dual-beam cantilever were $6 9 . 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , 113.9 $\mathrm { m V } ,$ and $0 . 3 0 3 \ \mu \mathrm { W } ,$ respectively, at optimal resistance and at $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { g }$ (gravitational acceleration, $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ . Based on these results, we fabricated cantilever devices using dual-beam cantilevers. The experimentally harvested power density of the dual-beam cantilever compared favorably with the simulated result. Experiments revealed the resonant frequency, voltage, and average power density to be $7 8 . 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ $1 1 8 . 5 \ \mathrm { m V } ,$ , and $0 . 3 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } _ { ; }$ , respectively. The error between the measured and simulated data is therefore approximately $10 \%$ . The maximum average power and average power density of the dual-beam cantilever produced at $_ { 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ were $0 . 8 0 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and $1 , 3 2 2 . 8 0 \ \mu \mathrm { W } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , respectively. We showed that the dual-beam cantilever has higher strain due to the blank area of beam center. Therefore, these results show much improvement over the results of previously published works and indicate the usefulness of low power energy-harvesting applications on the MEMS scale.
